abstract.p: This short elegy on the death of Queen Anne is framed as an appeal to Apollo (god of poetry). The speaker asks Apollo for inspiration to write even a single verse worthy of the queen’s death. He then elevates her importance by suggesting that if the Graces and the Muses themselves were dead and buried, they could be reborn “phoenix-like” from her ashes.

lg.l: Of Graces three, And Muses nine
Gentle daine mee one poore verse
To pinne upon this Sacred Herse;
For if Graces three were dead

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Anne of Denmark, queen consort of James I, died unexpectedly on 2 March 1619 at Hampton Court after a period of ill health. Her death prompted a wave of elegiac writing that, while less intense than that following the death of her son, Prince Henry, nonetheless reflects broader national anxieties and the developing conventions of mourning royal figures in the early Stuart period.(Doelman 2016)
